sections.title: Chemical foundations of life
sections.text:
Living systems use chemical compounds governed by the same physical laws as nonliving matter. Carbon can form four covalent bonds and build chains, rings and branched structures. Oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur and many other elements contribute essential functions. Water supports life through solvent properties, thermal behaviour and participation in reactions.

Carbohydrates include simple sugars and larger polymers. Glucose is a major fuel; starch stores carbohydrate in plants; glycogen stores it in animals; cellulose provides plant-cell-wall structure. Their biological behaviour differs because bond arrangement and branching affect interactions with enzymes. Humans digest accessible starch but lack digestive enzymes that efficiently hydrolyse cellulose into glucose.

Lipids are a diverse group including triglycerides, phospholipids and steroids. Triglycerides store energy, phospholipids form membranes and cholesterol participates in membrane structure and steroid synthesis. Lipids are not all chemically identical fats. Their hydrophobic regions are especially important in organizing cellular boundaries.

Proteins are amino-acid polymers joined by peptide bonds. Primary structure is the amino-acid sequence; secondary structure includes local helices and sheets; tertiary structure is overall folding; quaternary structure describes association of multiple polypeptide subunits when present. Structure supports functions including catalysis, transport, contraction and immune recognition. Heat or extreme pH can alter folding, producing denaturation without necessarily breaking every peptide bond. Food-related composition and nutritional examples are developed in Chapter 21.

sections.title: Enzyme action and regulation
sections.text:
An enzyme is a biological catalyst, usually a protein, that increases reaction rate by lowering the activation-energy barrier. A substrate binds to the active site, the enzyme facilitates chemical transformation and products are released. The enzyme is regenerated for another catalytic cycle. Binding often changes the enzyme's conformation; the active site is not necessarily an inflexible lock.

Enzymes do not supply unlimited energy or change a reaction's equilibrium constant at the same temperature. They speed forward and reverse reactions and permit biological chemistry to proceed under cellular conditions. Some need cofactors such as metal ions or coenzymes derived from vitamins. [OpenStax: enzymes](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/6-5-enzymes).

Reaction rate depends on temperature, pH, enzyme concentration and substrate availability. Increasing temperature can accelerate collisions but eventually damage structure. Each enzyme has a suitable operating range rather than one universal temperature optimum for all organisms. At high substrate concentration, active sites become occupied much of the time, so adding still more substrate produces diminishing increases in rate.

Reversible competitive inhibitors compete with substrate at an active site; sufficiently high substrate concentration can reduce their apparent effect in a simple model. Other inhibitors act through different sites or irreversible chemical changes. Feedback inhibition occurs when a pathway's product reduces an earlier enzyme's activity, helping prevent unnecessary production. Regulation makes metabolism coordinated rather than a collection of independent reactions.

sections.title: ATP and energy coupling
sections.text:
Metabolism includes catabolism, which breaks molecules down, and anabolism, which builds molecules. These pathways exchange energy and materials. ATP is a common cellular energy-transfer molecule. Hydrolysis of ATP can be coupled to otherwise unfavourable processes such as pumping ions or driving biosynthesis. It is misleading to say energy is released merely because a bond is broken: breaking a bond requires energy, while the overall reaction releases usable free energy because of the properties of all reactants and products.

Cells continually regenerate ATP from ADP and phosphate. They do not store their entire lifetime's energy as ATP. Long-term reserves such as triglycerides or glycogen supply fuels that support ATP regeneration. Energy transfer also involves electron carriers, notably NADH and FADH₂ in respiration and NADPH in many biosynthetic pathways.

sections.title: Aerobic respiration step by step
sections.text:
In glycolysis, a glucose molecule is converted into two pyruvate molecules in the cytosol, producing a small net ATP yield and reduced electron carriers. When aerobic mitochondrial metabolism proceeds, pyruvate is converted to acetyl-CoA, releasing carbon dioxide and generating NADH. The citric acid cycle oxidizes the acetyl group further, producing carbon dioxide, reduced carriers and a small amount of directly formed energy-transfer nucleotide.

Electrons from reduced carriers pass through an electron-transport chain in the inner mitochondrial membrane. Energy from these reactions supports proton movement across the membrane, establishing an electrochemical gradient. ATP synthase couples proton flow down this gradient to ATP formation. Oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor in ordinary aerobic respiration and is reduced to water. [OpenStax: oxidative phosphorylation](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/7-4-oxidative-phosphorylation).

The overall glucose equation is:

$$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6+6O_2\rightarrow6CO_2+6H_2O+energy}.$$

It balances material inputs and outputs but represents many reactions, not one cellular explosion. Energy is captured partly in ATP and transferred partly as heat. Actual ATP yield varies with cellular conditions and transport costs, so a single fixed yield should not be treated as universally exact.

When oxygen-dependent oxidation is unavailable, fermentation can regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis continues. Lactate fermentation and alcoholic fermentation produce different end products. Fermentation provides much less ATP per glucose than complete aerobic oxidation because much chemical energy remains in its products. Anaerobic respiration is a different process that uses an electron-transport chain with an acceptor other than oxygen in suitable organisms.

sections.title: Photosynthesis and plant energy
sections.text:
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy. In oxygenic photosynthesis, light reactions in chloroplast thylakoid membranes excite electrons, oxidize water, release oxygen and produce ATP and NADPH. Oxygen released into the atmosphere comes from water, not directly from carbon dioxide. The Calvin–Benson cycle in the stroma uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into organic intermediates. [OpenStax: light-dependent reactions](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/8-2-the-light-dependent-reactions-of-photosynthesis).

An introductory net representation is:

$$\mathrm{6CO_2+6H_2O+light\rightarrow C_6H_{12}O_6+6O_2}.$$

This is a simplified balance rather than a claim that a glucose molecule is the immediate product of one reaction. Light-independent carbon-fixation reactions depend on energy products of the light reactions and cellular regulation; calling them “dark reactions” does not mean they normally occur only at night.

Plants also perform cellular respiration. Photosynthesis makes organic material and captures light energy, while respiration releases usable energy from suitable fuels. In darkness a plant can continue producing mitochondrial ATP from stored organic compounds. Productivity depends on light, carbon dioxide, water, temperature and nutrient supply; increasing one factor cannot overcome every other limitation.

**Why membranes matter to energy production.** A proton gradient requires a barrier that limits uncontrolled ion movement. If a membrane becomes freely permeable to protons, electron transport may continue without efficiently driving ATP synthase because the stored gradient dissipates. This connects energy conversion with membrane structure and explains why organelles cannot be understood as isolated bags of enzymes. Energy is stored partly in an organized difference across a boundary.

**Metabolic flexibility.** Cells can use fatty acids and amino-acid carbon skeletons as well as glucose. These fuels enter central metabolism through appropriate pathways, while nitrogen from amino acids requires separate handling. A fuel's caloric content does not alone determine how rapidly a tissue can use it. Enzyme activity, oxygen delivery, transport and hormonal signals coordinate supply with demand.

**Photosynthetic limitation and water use.** Closing stomata during water stress reduces water loss but also restricts carbon dioxide entry. Temperature affects enzymes and respiratory demand, while leaf structure affects light capture. Some plants have adaptations that alter how carbon is acquired and concentrated. These strategies help explain ecological differences among plants, without changing the underlying need to balance carbon gain, water conservation and metabolic costs.

questions.prompt: A plant cell continues producing ATP in darkness using stored organic compounds. Which organelle is particularly important for this aerobic process?
questions.explanation: Plant mitochondria can produce ATP through aerobic cellular respiration even when photosynthesis is not occurring.

questions.prompt: During oxygenic photosynthesis, the molecular oxygen released into the atmosphere originates mainly from:

options.C: Water molecules split during the light reactions

questions.explanation: Oxygenic photosynthesis produces O₂ by water oxidation at photosystem II.

questions.prompt: In the chloroplast, the Calvin–Benson cycle primarily performs which operation?

options.B: Fixation of CO₂ into organic intermediates using ATP and NADPH
options.C: Translation of messenger RNA in mitochondria

questions.explanation: The Calvin–Benson cycle incorporates inorganic carbon into organic compounds, using products of the light reactions.

questions.prompt: A reversible competitive inhibitor binds an enzyme's active site. What often happens when substrate concentration is increased sufficiently in the simple model?

options.C: The reaction changes its equilibrium constant
options.D: Substrate can outcompete inhibitor, reducing the apparent inhibition

questions.explanation: Competitive inhibition can often be overcome at sufficiently high substrate concentration when reversible binding and simple kinetics apply.
